Note.Name: README for maintainers
Note.Text:
Technical Documentation

Overview

This implementation provides timing metrics in a survey by combining a client-side active timer with server-side aggregation.

The browser measures how long a respondent is actively engaged on each page. The server then decides how that time should be interpreted: how it contributes to global timings, which section it belongs to, and whether it should be retained for backend use.

The system produces three kinds of timing data:

  1. Global timings, covering the respondent’s overall survey session.

  2. Section-level timings, based on explicit section markers maintained by the script.

  3. Page-level timing records, stored in question_timings_json for backend and integration use.

The page-level JSON data is not intended as a researcher-facing output. It exists to support integrations, diagnostics, speed checks, and other backend processes that need access to submitted page timing records.

The result is not a perfect reconstruction of respondent behaviour, but a consistent and interpretable timing system that works across both CAWI and CATI modes. The existing documentation describes the client/server split and active-time model, while the updated code adds page-level JSON logging through updateQuestionTimingsJson(pageTimeRaw, date).

Core Concepts

Client and Server Responsibilities

The client measures active time on each page. It does not know anything about sections or survey structure. It simply records page-level timing information and sends it with each page submission.

The server is responsible for interpretation. It updates the global timing fields, assigns active time to the correct section, and appends the submitted page timing object to question_timings_json.

The key attribution rule is:

The time recorded on a page is assigned to the section that was just shown, not the section that is about to be shown.

This is why the system stores both the current section and the last rendered section.

Section State Model

Forsta does not track sections directly, so the script maintains its own section state using a stack stored in timestamp_section_stack.

The stack represents the section path the respondent has taken. The current section is always the last item in the stack.

When the respondent moves forward, a new section is pushed onto the stack. When the respondent moves backwards and the same section marker is encountered again, the most recent section is popped from the stack.

This approach depends on section markers being encountered consistently. Markers do not have to be unconditional, but the survey paths must be symmetric: if a respondent reaches a section through a given route, they must encounter the same markers when backtracking along that route.

Execution Flow

When a respondent moves through the survey, two functions do most of the work.

First, setTimestampSection(n) is called at explicit section boundaries. It updates timestamp_section_stack and increments the visit count for the section that has just been entered.

Second, runTimestampUpdate() executes once per rendered page. This call is placed in the global page theme HTML rather than global question validation, because validation runs once per question and there may be multiple questions on a page.

runTimestampUpdate() performs four tasks:

  1. It reads and parses the submitted pageTime payload from the request form.

  2. It appends the raw timing object to question_timings_json, if the payload is valid.

  3. It updates the global start time, end time, and active duration.

  4. It updates section-level start time, end time, and active duration using the current and last rendered sections.

Section Timing Logic

Each section has three timing values: start time, end time, and active duration.

The start time is the first time the respondent enters the section. Once set, it does not change.

The end time is the first time the respondent leaves the section. This includes both forward and backward movement. It is not updated if the respondent later returns, so it should not be treated as a completion time.

The active duration is the total active time attributed to the section. If a respondent visits a section more than once, the active time from each visit is added together.

Active duration will often differ from the difference between start time and end time because idle time is excluded and respondents may revisit sections.

Page-Level Timing JSON

The system also stores a page-level timing history in question_timings_json.

This field contains a JSON array. Each item represents one submitted page timing payload. For example:

[
  {
    "pageId": "i278",
    "startTime": "2026-05-27T03:15:41.183Z",
    "activeSeconds": 2,
    "submitTime": "2026-05-27T03:15:43.705Z"
  },
  {
    "pageId": "i279",
    "startTime": "2026-05-27T03:15:46.664Z",
    "activeSeconds": 2,
    "submitTime": "2026-05-27T03:15:54.688Z"
  }
]

The fields are:

Field Meaning
pageId Identifies the submitted page or rendered question context.
startTime Client-side timestamp for when timing began on that page.
activeSeconds Active time accumulated by the client-side timer.
submitTime Server-side timestamp added when the page submission is processed.

question_timings_json is intended for backend and integration use. It may be useful for speed checks, diagnostic review, or integrations that need page-level timing events rather than section-level aggregates.

It should not be treated as a replacement for the global or section timing fields. The global and section fields are the interpreted timing outputs. The JSON array is a lower-level submission log.

The implementation only appends to question_timings_json when the submitted timing payload is a non-empty object. If the payload is missing, invalid, or empty, no page-level record is added.

Active and Idle Time

The client-side timer estimates active engagement using simple heuristics.

Time is counted when the page is in focus and the respondent has interacted recently with the page. Mouse movement, clicks, and key presses reset the idle counter.

If there is no interaction for 60 seconds, the page is treated as idle and time stops accumulating. Timing also stops when the browser window loses focus.

These rules are approximate. A respondent who is reading without interacting for more than 60 seconds may be counted as idle. A respondent making occasional small interactions may continue to be counted as active. The timings should therefore be interpreted as estimates of active interaction, not exact measures of attention.

Important Assumptions

This implementation assumes that:

  1. Section boundaries are explicitly defined using setTimestampSection(n).

  2. Section markers are encountered consistently when moving forwards and backwards.

  3. Forsta re-executes script nodes when navigating backwards.

  4. The client submits a valid timing payload when page-level JSON logging is required.

  5. question_timings_json contains either no value or a valid JSON array managed by this script.

Manual edits or malformed values in question_timings_json may prevent the page-level log from updating correctly, so the field should be treated as system-managed backend data.

Known Limitations

End times do not represent section completion. They represent the first time the respondent leaves a section.

Active duration does not equal elapsed time between start and end. Idle time is excluded, and respondents may revisit sections.

The section stack is not a full navigation history. It represents the current traversal state, not every movement through the survey.

question_timings_json provides page-level submission records, but it does not by itself explain the respondent’s route through the survey or resolve page timings into sections. That interpretation still depends on the section stack and section timing logic.

Because question_timings_json grows during the interview, it should be treated as backend support data rather than a normal reporting variable.

Why This Design Was Chosen

The design favours simple, interpretable timing rules over a full reconstruction of respondent behaviour.

The section-level fields provide stable, researcher-usable timing metrics. The page-level JSON log preserves more granular timing events for backend systems that need them.

Keeping these outputs separate avoids overloading the researcher-facing timing variables while still making the underlying page submission data available for integrations and diagnostics.

Note.Name: README for programmers
Note.Text:
Survey Programmer Documentation

Overview

This timing system is designed to be simple to implement in a survey, but it depends on section markers being placed correctly. As a survey programmer, your job is mainly to define where sections begin. The timing logic itself is handled by the underlying scripts.

In practice, the system records when respondents first enter a section, when they first leave it, and how much active time they spend in it. It also handles backtracking, provided section markers are encountered consistently in both directions.

What You Need to Do

To use the system, place a call to setTimestampSection(n) at the start of each section, where n is the section identifier. These calls define the boundaries the timing system uses.

Each section number should be unique within the survey. The numbering does not need any special meaning beyond identifying one section from another, but it does need to be consistent.

You do not need to calculate timings yourself or update timing variables manually. Once the markers are in place, the client-side and server-side code handle the rest.

Placement Rules

The main requirement is that section markers must be encountered consistently along any route a respondent can take through the survey. They do not have to be unconditional in every case, but the routing must be symmetric. If a respondent reaches a section through a particular path, then when they backtrack they must encounter the same markers again in the reverse order.

In practical terms, this means you should place setTimestampSection(n) calls at genuine section boundaries and avoid placing them in ways that could cause them to be skipped on the way forward or on the way back.

If the marker structure is inconsistent, timings may be assigned to the wrong section.

If you place setTimestampSection(n) calls only at the top level of the survey script (not nested within call blocks or if blocks), then this requirement will be met. 

Summary

To implement the system correctly, define each section boundary with setTimestampSection(n) and make sure those markers are encountered consistently across the survey flow. Once that is in place, the timing scripts will handle start times, end times, active durations, and backtracking automatically.

FormText.Text:
Thank you for your interest in the Graduate Outcomes Survey. This is an important survey conducted by the Social Research Centre on behalf of The Australian Government Department of Education, which aims to measure graduate satisfaction and employment outcomes.

The Graduate Outcomes Survey is the largest Australian study of graduates and the only source of national data on graduate experiences with higher education. As a recent graduate, we are very interested to hear how things are going for you since completing your course, even if you are not currently working.

Participation in this survey is voluntary. You are not obligated to answer any or all of the questions and you can choose to stop at any time. Your responses will be completely confidential and used only for the purposes of this research. Only aggregated, non-identifiable data are made publicly available.

The survey takes approximately ^f('IntLength')^ minutes to complete, depending on your answers.

If you need to take a break, you can press the ‘Save and close’ button and close your browser. You can come back to the survey at any time and continue from where you stopped.

Please do not use the browser ‘BACK’ button to go back to a previous question.

The Department of Education’s Graduate Outcomes Survey Privacy Notice provides detailed information about the collection and use of your personal information for the purposes of this research. By participating in the GOS, you consent to the handling of your personal information in accordance with this privacy notice.

FormText.Text: Next, we would like to understand what you are currently doing in terms of work and study. A number of questions may seem similar, however these items are based on the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) Labour Force Survey. Using the ABS approach means the information you provide is more robust and able to be compared to national employment statistics.

FormText.Text: Even though you are not currently working, would you like a paid job of any kind at the moment?

Texts.Text: Yes, I could start within 4 weeks if work was available

FormText.Text:
At any time during the last 4 weeks have you been looking for full-time work?

Please note:

  • ‘Actively looking for work' includes written, telephoned or applied to an employer; had an interview with an employer for work; answered an advertisement for a job; checked or registered with an employment agency; taken steps to purchase or start your own business; advertised or tendered for work; and contacted friends or relatives to find work.
  • ‘Passively looking for work’ includes only looking in newspapers, the internet, or notice boards, and not taking any specific action to obtain work from these sources.

Texts.Text: Yes, I have been actively looking for full-time work
Yes, I have been passively looking for full-time work

FormText.Text:
Have you been looking for part-time work at any time during the last 4 weeks?

Please note:

  • ‘Actively looking for work' includes written, telephoned or applied to an employer; had an interview with an employer for work; answered an advertisement for a job; checked or registered with an employment agency; taken steps to purchase or start your own business; advertised or tendered for work; and contacted friends or relatives to find work.
  • ‘Passively looking for work’ includes only looking in newspapers, the internet, or notice boards, and not taking any specific action to obtain work from these sources.

Texts.Text: Yes, I have been actively looking for part-time work
Yes, I have been passively looking for part-time work

FormText.Text:
Last week, were you waiting to start paid work you had already obtained?

Please note ‘work you had already obtained’ refers to new types of work that you have acquired but not yet commenced. This includes waiting for a graduate role to commence.
If you had found a job, could you have started last week?

You mentioned that you didn’t look for work during the last 4 weeks. Was that because you were waiting to start work you had already obtained?

Please note ‘work you had already obtained’ refers to new types of work that you have acquired but not yet commenced. This includes waiting for a graduate role to commence.
Will you be starting that work in the next 4 weeks?

FormText.Text:
The following questions have been included by the Australian Government Department of Education to gather feedback on your Initial Teacher Education (ITE) experience.

Your feedback will help develop a better understanding of people’s experiences in ITE, offering valuable insights into what graduate teachers have learnt in their ITE programs and how confident they feel applying this knowledge in classroom settings.

The findings from this research will inform how quality teacher education can be provided to students and how ^f('HEPTYPE_TXT')^ can best prepare teachers for the workforce.

FormText.Title: ITE1
FormText.Text: Which of the following specialisation(s) did you study as part of your ^f('DoubleCourse')^?

FormText.Title: ITEOUT
FormText.Text: Thank you for your responses. We are only seeking the experiences of graduates who completed studies in primary or secondary education, please proceed to the next section of the survey.

FormText.Title: ITE4INTRO
FormText.Text:
The following questions seek your views about what you learnt in your ^f('ITECOURSEA')^ (specialising in ^(f('ITECOURSEA_FLAG').any('0')?(f('ITE1a').toBoolean()?f('ITE1a'):""):(f('ITE1b').toBoolean() ? f('ITE1b'): ""))^). Please reflect specifically on your ITE program and its impact on your teaching knowledge and skills.

As much as possible, your responses should focus on your ITE program, and avoid experiences from outside your degree (e.g., personal study, previous career, teaching experiences post-graduation).

FormText.Title: ITE4
FormText.Text: Based on what you learned during your ITE program, how knowledgeable do you feel about the following…

Texts.Text: Differences between ‘novice’ and ‘expert’ learners, including how instruction should be adapted to effectively support each learner type
How learning occurs, including the role of memory and effective instruction in reducing cognitive overload
How a ‘novice’ learner progresses to ‘expert’ learner, including the need to adjust instruction as they progress to independent practice and problem-solving
How myths about the way people learn can hinder effective instruction (e.g., belief that people are either “left-brained” or “right-brained”)
Multi-tiered systems of support (MTSS), including evidence-informed teaching that is a key part of this
Methods and strategies for promoting positive student behaviour and engagement (e.g., clear and consistent expectations, constructive feedback)
Whole-school behaviour frameworks, including whole-school approaches to promote positive behaviour
First Nations diversity and perspectives in the curriculum and practical examples of how to authentically engage with local First Nations peoples
Culturally responsive practices, including understanding and valuing cultural diversity, and affirming First Nations students and students with English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D)
Effective ways that teachers can collaborate with families of diverse backgrounds to support students at different stages of learning and development
Evidence-informed teaching practices that support learning among diverse students, including those with additional needs, disability, or from disadvantaged backgrounds

FormText.Title: ITE5
FormText.Text: Based on what you learned during your ITE program, how confident would you be to undertake the following as a practising teacher in your own classroom next week …

Texts.Text: Regularly plan and sequence learning with gradually more challenging content and tasks, including spacing and retrieval practices to help students remember what they learn
Regularly apply explicit teaching, modelling, and scaffolding practices that support students to learn effectively and reduce cognitive overload
Select a range of evidence-informed assessment strategies as a regular part of teaching practice to evaluate student progress, provide targeted feedback, and adjust teaching as appropriate
Effectively teach literacy, including explicit teaching of reading and writing tailored to discipline-specific curriculum (e.g. phonics, comprehension)
Deliver explicit instruction for reading to align with the cognitive processes that build phonemic awareness, fluency, vocabulary, etc.
Deliver explicit instruction in reading and writing that is tailored to discipline-specific curriculum and content
Effectively apply explicit numeracy instruction, including strategies to build mathematical fluency, problem solving, and reasoning
Teach across the six strands of mathematics (number, algebra, geometry, measurement, statistics, probability), including the four proficiencies (understanding, fluency, problem solving, reasoning)
Deliver explicit numeracy instruction, with removal of scaffolding as students move towards mastery of mathematical concepts and skills (numerical, spatial, graphical, statistical, algebraic)
Incorporate independent practice and problem-solving as students master foundational mathematical knowledge and skills
Consistently apply rules and routines to help support a structured, safe, and positive classroom environment (e.g., reinforcement of rules, entry and exit routines)
Consistently apply practices to promote high expectations, good interpersonal relationships, and positive personalised goals for students’ behaviour
Manage classroom behaviour through calm and consistent responses, including modelling and feedback emphasising positive behaviours

Descriptions.Description: MODULE H: INITIAL TEACHER EDUCATION (ITE) MODULE

FormText.Title: NAHGOTINT
FormText.Text:
The Nursing and Allied Health Graduate Outcome Tracking (NAHGOT) study is a collaborative research project being undertaken by Monash University, University of Newcastle, Deakin University, University of Southern Queensland, The University of Queensland, Charles Sturt University, James Cook University, La Trobe University, Flinders University, University of Tasmania, and Adelaide University.

As a graduate of a health discipline, you are invited to complete the following questions as part of this study. It seeks to understand the association between a student’s rural/urban background, practice location intention, and university placement experience, and how this influences your choice of workplace.

Further information can be found on the NAHGOT website here.

FormText.Text:
Work-Integrated Learning Australia (WIL Australia) is a not-for-profit national body whose members are Australian higher education and vocational education institutions.

WIL Australia has included the following questions about your participation in work-integrated learning, related employability activities and paid work during your studies, and your views on how these influenced your outcomes after graduating.

As with items included by your institution, answering these questions is voluntary. You are not obliged to answer any or all of them and you can stop at any time.

If you answer them, your responses are collected by the Social Research Centre, which provides WIL Australia with a dataset containing your responses. It does not include your name or contact details. WIL Australia uses this for national research and reporting on work-integrated learning, including aggregate reports, sector submissions and peer-reviewed research. WIL Australia does not publish findings that identify individual graduates.

How WIL Australia handles this information is set out in the WIL Australia GOS Privacy and Data Use Notice available on their website: https://wilaustralia.edu.au/wil-in-gos/.
